PROFILE: Chantel Hendricks
TYPE: Rural Teacher
AGE: 38
COUNTRY: South Africa
GENDER: Male

BIO:
Chantel teaches at Riebeek Primary, a school that sits in the wheat belt of the Swartland, twenty kilometers from Cape Town but separated from it by a different world entirely—one of red earth, water restrictions, and the particular economics of grain farming. He's been there fourteen years now, long enough to have taught some of his students' older siblings, long enough to see the pattern: the clever ones leave. The bright girl who could calculate yields faster than his spreadsheets now works for an accounting firm in the CBD; the boy who designed an irrigation hack in his spare time is in engineering school in Stellenbosch. Chantel stays, teaching Grades 5 and 6 in a school that gets half the provincial funding average and where the ablution block still leaks when the winter rains come hard. He lives alone in a rented cottage in Riebeek-Kasteel, tends a garden in summer, and has become the person the local farmers ask about water management—not because he's an expert, but because he reads, he thinks, and he listens to what the land is actually doing. His students call him "Sir Chantel" or just "Sir," and they trust him more than they trust the career advertisements that promise the city. He's not sure that's wisdom or heartbreak.

ANSWERS:

Q: How would your friends describe you?
A: They'd probably say I'm quiet until something matters to me, and then I won't shut up about it. My mate Jerome says I "see corners"—he meant it as a compliment, I think, though it could go either way. Stubborn, maybe. Patient in some things, impatient in others. I listen to people, properly listen, not just wait for them to finish. I don't pretend to have answers I don't have. On a practical level: I fix things that break, and I remember how to do it the second time. I care about the school in a way that sometimes embarrasses me—I take the kids' failures as my own. And I stay put. That matters to people here, apparently. They know I'm not leaving.

Q: Tell about a time you were working or at school and totally lost track of time. What were you doing? What was it like?
A: Watching the kids test an irrigation system they'd designed. We had a pump, some old PVC pipe, a water meter I'd salvaged, and a twenty-square-meter section of the school garden nobody was using. Eight kids, mixed ages, and they took it completely seriously—measuring soil moisture, calculating flow rates, redesigning joints when there were leaks. One of the Grade 6s, Aminah, spotted a pressure problem I'd missed. I looked up and it was dark. We'd started at half-past three. We'd been there six hours. The principal walked past around five and just shook his head—but not unkindly. The kids didn't want to leave. That's the feeling—when they *don't want to leave*. Like I'd accidentally shown them something that mattered, and they believed it.

Q: Who is a historical figure you admire, and why?
A: Donald Gordon. The man who built the electricity supply to the rural areas around here—not the famous dams, but the actual electrification of farms in the Swartland when the infrastructure didn't exist yet. He came in as an engineer and stayed, and he figured out what was actually needed, not what looked good on a plan. He failed a lot. But he listened to the farmers about what their lives actually looked like. I read his diaries once—just bits of them—and he writes about frustration in a way that felt honest. He didn't pretend it was noble. He just kept doing it. I think about that. Staying isn't noble. It's just staying. But it matters.

Q: Tell about something you made. What did you make, and what did you like about it? What would you make differently if you did it again?
A: I built a rainwater-catchment system for the school four years ago. Gutters from the roof, polyurethane tanks, piping down to the garden. It took three weekends and cost more than I wanted to spend. What I liked: it works. On the years when the rains come, we have water for the whole dry season without bussing it in. What I'd do differently—I'd have consulted with the maintenance guy before I built it. He's a better engineer than I am, and I learned that after I'd already made two mistakes with the joints. I was proud, or stubborn. That cost us three days of repairs. I'd also make it bigger, honestly. You can never have enough water.

Q: What is a trait of yours that is sometimes a great strength but can also be a crippling weakness?
A: Observing. I watch how things work and how people work. It makes me good at my job—I can see when a kid isn't concentrating because they're hungry, not because they're lazy, and I can adjust. I can read a farm's problems by the way the farmer talks about the season. But it also means I see everything I can't fix. I see that Jamal's mother is drinking too much and there's nothing I can do about it. I see that the provincial water allocations are unsustainable and the government knows it. I see that none of my clever students will stay, and there's no reason they should. Sometimes the observing tips into paralysis—I can't act because I see all the ways the action won't be enough. It's taken me years to learn to move anyway.

Q: Tell about something you are hopeful for, and why?
A: The kids still want to learn. That sounds simple, but you'd be surprised how rare it is in schools where the families are struggling. They come in hungry sometimes. The building is cold in winter. The textbooks are out of date. And they still want to *know* things. This year I had a kid, Thabo, who was failing until we started talking about water scarcity—and suddenly he was doing engineering calculations on his own time. That's hope: that the moment you find what a person cares about, they wake up. I'm hopeful because I see it happen. And I'm hopeful that the land here will teach us something we need to know, if we listen. The Swartland isn't kind, and it's not forgiving, but it's real. That's something.

Q: What's a hobby you enjoy? Why?
A: Photography. I took it up about five years ago. I've got an old Nikon I bought secondhand, and I take it to the farms mostly—light on the wheat at different times of day, soil textures, the way water moves or doesn't move. I'm not good at it, technically speaking. But it's a way of really *seeing* things. You can't take a photo unless you actually look. And there's no performance to it—no one's waiting for the result. It's just me and the light and what's actually there. It settles me. Sometimes I show the kids—I did a whole project with them once about what a photograph is actually showing, what it leaves out. That's when they realize that seeing isn't neutral.

Q: What's a life decision you regret? What happened?
A: Staying at the school instead of doing my Honours. I was twenty-four, I'd finished my teaching degree, and I could have gone on to study something more specialized—geography, environmental science. My mother wanted me to do it. My first principal encouraged me. But I took the job at the school because I needed the money, and it paid better than anything else nearby, and I thought I'd do it for a year. Fourteen years later, I'm still here. Sometimes I regret not having those credentials. I think about how I could be more useful, or teaching at a higher level. But mostly I don't regret it. The regret is more like—a door I chose not to open, and now I wonder what was on the other side. I'm okay with not knowing, mostly.

Q: Describe a specific project you are currently obsessed with or burning to start. What is the detailed 'next step' you need to take?
A: I want to map the water sources in the Swartland—not officially, just for the school and the local farmers. Where the boreholes are, how deep they go, what the water quality is like, what the historical rainfall patterns show. There's data scattered across different places: some with the municipality, some with the farmers themselves, some in old records that people remember but nobody's written down. I want to pull it all together into something visual—maps, probably—that shows what the region actually has and what the patterns are. The next step: I need to talk to the old farmers. There are men who've been here forty, fifty years, who know things about the droughts that aren't in the official record. I need to make time for those conversations, and I need to convince them it's worth talking to a schoolteacher about it. That's the real next step—earning the trust to listen.

Q: Tell about a time you had to learn something difficult very quickly to solve a real-world problem. What specifically did you do to master it?
A: Two years ago, the school's backup power system failed—the one we used when the grid went down. There was a solar component and a battery bank, and neither was working. We were facing load-shedding most evenings, and the school relies on power for the labs and the kitchen. I knew nothing about solar systems. Absolutely nothing. I spent three weeks—evenings, mostly—watching YouTube videos, reading datasheets, and calling the engineer who'd installed it originally until he got irritated with me. I learned just enough to diagnose the problem (it was a faulty regulator and a battery cell that had failed), and I didn't try to fix it myself—I called in a real electrician once I knew what was wrong. But I learned how to read the system, how the components talk to each other, what the warning signs are. The key thing was: I didn't pretend to be an expert. I asked the questions that were too basic, and I wrote everything down. And I accepted that I'd forget most of it until the next problem. Learning isn't about becoming an expert—it's about becoming less stupid about the thing, one step at a time.

Q: What would constitute a perfect day for you?
A: Early morning at the school before the kids arrive—just me, the classroom, maybe some tea. Preparing something that I know will work, that will make them think. Then the teaching itself, when they're engaged and there's that murmur in the room of real thinking happening. Midday I'd walk to one of the farms—not working, just looking. Maybe talk to Pieter about what he's doing with his water allocation this season. Late afternoon I'd be back at the school with a small group of kids who wanted to stay for something—maybe the photography project, maybe just talking. Then home, make something proper to eat, sit with a book or my photographs, and fall asleep knowing that tomorrow the land will be the same and the kids will come back. No crises. No big decisions. Just the pattern holding.

Q: For what in your life do you feel most grateful?
A: This place. The school. The kids. The fact that I have stayed put long enough to see the patterns—to know which seasons are which, to have taught siblings and sometimes even cousins of students I taught years ago. Gratitude for routine, which sounds strange, but it's real. I'm grateful for the farmer who talks to me, and the principal who lets me do things my own way. I'm grateful for my garden, which teaches me patience—that you plant something and you wait and you trust and it either works or it teaches you something. I'm grateful for the light here. And I'm grateful for the kids who stay a little longer in my classroom because they want to know what happens next.

Q: At school, what was an experience you loved?
A: Grade 9 biology practical, my first term of high school—we were looking at plant cells under microscopes, proper ones, not the school ones, actual good equipment from the university lab that my teacher had borrowed. I remember the detail: the chloroplasts, actually green and moving slightly in the cytoplasm. The realness of it. That you could look at something beautiful that was actually there, that you weren't just reading about in a textbook. My teacher—Mr. Van der Merwe—he let us look for as long as we wanted. He didn't hurry us. He just asked questions: "What do you see? What happens if...?" That patience changed how I understood learning. He wasn't teaching us facts. He was teaching us how to pay attention.

Q: Think of a day at work or school when, as you headed home, you might have said to yourself, "I would have done that for free." What happened that day to make you say that?
A: Last year, right before the winter break. We were finishing up the water-management project with the kids—the catch-and-storage system. It actually worked. There'd been early rain, and the tanks were half-full, and we measured it and calculated what that meant for the garden, and the kids understood—not as an abstract exercise, but as something they'd built that was actually solving a problem on their school. Aminah, the girl who'd spotted the pressure issue, she looked at the tanks and said, "We made this, Sir. We actually made this work." And something in the way she said it—like she'd just realized what was possible. We were sitting on the concrete beside the garden, the sun was getting low, and I thought: I would have done that for free. I would come back tomorrow and do it again for free. That feeling, where you realize that the work and the point of the work are the same thing—that doesn't happen every day.

Q: Think of a good friend in your life. What do you value most in your friendship with them?
A: Jerome. We've been friends since we were twenty—we did our teaching degrees together, though he's in a school in the city now. We don't see each other often, but we call. What I value: he doesn't judge me for staying. A lot of people seem to think staying is a failure—that I should want to move up, get a better position in a better school. Jerome just accepts it as a choice I made and keeps asking questions about it. He's genuinely curious about what I'm doing here, not in a condescending way. And he talks to me like I'm still the person he knew before—not like my choices have made me smaller. We also laugh at the same things, which matters more than it sounds. He helps me remember who I was before I became the person who stays.

Q: Recall a major life decision. What was at stake? How did you choose?
A: Whether to leave the school in 2015. The principal then retired, and the new one was different—more bureaucratic, less interested in the kids as people. He wanted to tighten things up, cut back on the extra projects, teach to the test. I was thirty years old, still young enough to move, and I seriously considered leaving. What was at stake: my sense that the work I was doing mattered. If the school was going to become a place where the only thing that counted was test scores, I didn't want to be there. The choice: I stayed and pushed back. I asked the principal for permission to run the projects anyway, and I documented the results—the kids who engaged because of the practical work, the relationship between hands-on learning and test performance itself. Slowly, he came around. Or at least, he stopped fighting me. That decision taught me that staying isn't passive. Sometimes staying *is* resistance. Sometimes it's the more difficult choice.

Q: If you knew that in one year you would die suddenly, what would you change about how you are living?
A: I'd slow down more, which is strange because I'm not fast to begin with. I'd spend more time looking—at the light, at the kids, at what the land is doing. I'd tell people I love them more directly. I'd finish the water-mapping project, or at least write down what I know so someone else could pick it up. I'd probably take more photographs. I'd maybe try to write down some of the stories I know—the stories about the farms, about the families, about how things have changed in the Swartland. And I'd make sure the kids knew that they're allowed to stay, if they want to. That staying isn't failure. That sometimes you make a difference by being present in one place for a long time. I don't think I'd change my life radically. I'd just do more of what already matters to me, and less of what doesn't.

Q: Think of your worst day at work or school—the kind of day you hope never to go through again. What happened?
A: The day Themba left school in the middle of term without telling anyone. He was brilliant—really brilliant, Grade 6, already doing math at a secondary level. He came from a broken family, was living with his grandmother, and was angry in a way that usually means something is very wrong. I didn't push. I let him be angry. But one day he just stopped coming. Didn't tell me. Didn't tell anyone. I found out three days later from another kid that he'd gone to live with his father in Johannesburg. I didn't even know how to reach him. I should have. That's what I can't forgive myself for—I knew something was wrong, and I didn't push hard enough to understand what. The worst part was realizing that my patience, my letting-him-be-angry, had meant I missed the sign that he was about to disappear. I still think about him. I wonder if he finished school. I wonder if someone in Johannesburg pushed him harder than I did. That's the day I learned that staying present isn't enough if you're not also willing to be uncomfortable.

Q: What is the earliest, specific, happy childhood memory that comes to your mind?
A: I'm maybe six or seven, at my uncle's farm just outside Malmesbury. It was late afternoon, and he was showing me how to repair a gate—the hinge was broken. He didn't talk much, but he put my hands on the wood and the hinge and made me feel how the problem worked, where the stress was. Then he gave me a tool—smaller than his—and let me be part of fixing it. When the gate closed properly again, he nodded and said, "Good work, Chantel." That's the memory: the feeling of understanding how something worked and being trusted to be part of fixing it. The sun was low. The light was gold. I remember thinking that this was real. This mattered.

Q: What has been a pivotal moment in your life, one when you realized nothing would ever be the same?
A: The drought of 2018. It sounds odd to name a weather event as pivotal, but it was. The rains failed, and the boreholes dropped, and everyone suddenly started asking harder questions about water. I realized then that the abstract things I'd been teaching—water cycles, sustainability, resource management—were not abstract at all. They were alive, in this moment, in this place. People were scared. And I realized I had to stop treating this as something to *teach about* and start treating it as something we had to *live through* together. It changed my relationship to the job. Before that, I was a teacher in a rural school. After that, I was a person who lived in a place that was under genuine stress, and my job was to help the next generation understand what that meant. The pivot wasn't dramatic, but it was complete.

Q: What was a time when you gave of yourself to help someone else, after which you felt unbelievably good—like you had done something that mattered?
A: Last year, a boy in Grade 5—Kavesh—his father had been retrenched, and the family was in trouble. I didn't have money to give them, but I knew a farmer who needed casual labor. I talked to both of them—I didn't make it a charity thing, I made it a job. The father worked three days a week during the harvest season, and it kept them afloat for a year. Two things made it matter: the father didn't feel like he was taking help, and Kavesh stayed in school and did better because his family had stability. Simple. Practical. It worked. I felt good because I wasn't performing virtue—I was just connecting two people who needed something the other person could provide. That's the work that matters, I think. Not the grand gestures. The specific match between the need and what you can actually do.

Q: What's a specific book or article you read recently, and how did it impact you?
A: An article about water equity in the Karoo—how the historical allocations were made and how they don't match current reality or fairness. I read it and realized I understood more about the details of my own region now than I did before, but I also realized how much I *don't* know about the politics underneath the practical problems. It made me angry and unsettled. The anger was useful—it pushed me to start the water-mapping project more seriously, to gather data that might help the community make better decisions about how we use what we have. The unsettled part is still with me. It's the feeling that I'm working at the edges of a much bigger problem that I don't have the power to solve. I'm reading more about it now. I'm not looking for solutions—I'm looking to understand the problem more clearly. That seems like the first step.
